content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper is trying to tackle the problem that in recommender systems embeddings for infrequent items are not updated frequently and often it is hard to get high-quality embeddings for those items. The method proposed by the authors is to introduce the inner product for the embedding layer and is called multi-layer embeddings training (MLET).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The experiments done are very comprehensive and can support the effectiveness of the method.
2. The problem the paper trying to solve is important problem and the proposed method can mitigate the over-parameterization problem.

Weakness:
1. The presentation of the work is not very clear sometimes, for example, I am not entirely sure why the authors want to convey in Figure 1a. Why MLET we do not have dimension 128?
2. The idea makes sense to me, but it is not that novel. The idea has been floating around in the matrix factorization works for many years.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality of the paper is good, but the clarity and originality of the work is on the borderline.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think this paper is around borderline, the originality of the work is a bit weak but the experiments are well performed to support the effectiveness of the method.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
**Summary**

This paper explores a method/scheme called multi-layer embedding training (MLET). The authors claimed that MLET is a simple yet effective overparameterization method, which enables training-time factorization of linear embedding layers to enhance cross-entropy learning. Specifically, MLET trains embeddings via a sequence of two linear layers, instead of a single one.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Main Review**

Strength:

1. The idea is straightforward and simple. 
2. The results show good improvement according to Section 3 Experiments
3. Although the authors did not explicitly mention about practical applications, but I believe it’s worth exploring to have more discussions 


Weaknesses: 

1. Although the idea of the paper is simple, I personally found that the writing needs to improve a lot. For example, the authors could start with giving some definitions of what is “training-time factorization”, what is “enhancement factor of embedding update directions”, or what is “non-homogeneous weighting”. The current writing style makes it a bit hard to follow in my opinion. It appears to me that Section 2.1 is the only main contribution of the paper.
2. Section 2.3 and 2.4 are more important but they were also poorly written. In addition, most importantly, these sections did not provide a clear explanation of why factorization helps. Is it because of similar effects as SVD or anything else? It seems to me that the proposed method is just another embedding approach and somehow it works without concrete explanations.
3. With this type of contribution, I believe it will be more interesting to the readers if the authors discuss more about the practical aspects of the proposed method. Also, comparing with tensor-train decomposition methods (e.g., TT-Rec) are more relevant and interesting.
4. Minor: Appendix A.1 and A.2 are redundant in my opinion. Appendix A.4.1, A.4.2, A.4.3 are more interesting in terms of practical applications. The authors should emphasize more on this and perhaps even compare MLET to compression techniques. At the current version, Section 3.3 is too shallow.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality and clarity is okay but not so good. This work seems to be heavily inherit from tensor-train decomposition line of work
content.summary_of_the_review: All in all, although the idea is simple, the paper requires more work in order to convince the readers about its contributions.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper designs an effective overparameterization technique for enhancing recommendation model embedding training. Specifically, it uses training-time forced factorization of the embedding (linear) layer that enables cross-category learning. The proposed scheme, called multi-layer embedding training (MLET), converts the trained two-layer embedding into a single-layer one before deployment for inference. Evaluation results on two public click-through rate (CTR) prediction datasets have demonstrated better performance in terms of AUC and Logloss metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. Embedding learning for sparse features in recommendation models is an important research problem that has not been well explored but with promising value. 

2. The paper is generally easy to follow.

Weaknesses:

1. The biggest problem of this paper is the unrealistic problem setting of leveraging overparameterization in embedding learning. The proposed MLET use the larger inner dimension k in training and argue that the efficiency improves because the embedding dimension d is smaller than k. This is incorrect because training efficiency is equally important for recommendation models.

2. The motivation behind this scheme is quite unclear. If this paper aims to solve the model compression problem for large-embedding-size recommendation models, more experimental results should be presented in the main paper. Currently, it is more like using overparameterization, i.e., increasing model size, to improve the prediction accuracy, which, as commented above, is unrealistic for recommendation models.

3. Generality of the proposed MLET is also questionable, given the presented experimental results. For example, other non-DLRM models are only tested on the Avazu dataset because of run time issues, while most papers in this field do not have this issue. Also, using all default model parameters from the DeepCTR implementations is quite arbitrary.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There exists a large room for improving clarity. For example,

- Figure 1b is introduced before the Figure 1a

- All references are cited using the format of narrative citation. Many of them should use the format of the parenthetical citation. 

As for the novelty, although existing methods have only considered underparameterization in embedding learning instead of overparameterization, I can't entirely agree with its novelty given the unrealistic assumption behind this design.

Since no code is provided, I do not check its reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the listed weaknesses and other comments on clarity and novelty, I stand for the rejection for this paper.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present an approach that learns an embedding layer via a factorization approach in order to improve sparse updates when using a one layer for embeddings. The authors provide some theoretical evidence of why we would expect to have better performance. In the experimental part they enhance different state-of-the-art approaches and present results on two datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This is an interesting approach and generally the authors provide some good arguments and motivation. The experiments show some uplift in terms of the different metrics when using the MLET approach for learning the embeddings.

One important downside of the paper is the overall description. The authors refer to a model called DLRM without presenting it. There is figure but to be honest I cannot make much of it. A description would help as in the paper DLRM is used quite a lot. Also, the description of the experimental part is not very clear. The authors do not provide important  implementation details like for example of how exactly MLET is applied. They mention in the beginning that one can drop the two matrices W1 and W2 after obtaining W. Is this the case for the experiments? This is not clear in the text.

Because if it is not the case you just compare models that have an extra layer.

There are some choices like the following that the authors do not explain: "All DLRM results are the mean of five
training runs. Results from the other models are the mean of three training runs". Why is that?

Other examples:
- "we train all models for a single epoch". You cite a paper but not explain why.
- Similar to all the choices for learning rates etc. 

In section 3.2 it is unclear how you created these two datasets with the 10% most/less frequent.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper needs improvement when describing the approach as well as the experimental part. In some parts (as per comments) is very confusing. I am not sure that someone can reproduce the results using the described experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: Generally this is an interesting paper, even though the exact application of the approach was not clearly described. The authors provide theoretical evidence to support their claims. Despite that the experimental part is not well described which makes very hard to assess this approach.
